title: When Discipling Gets Hard
subtitle: Five sessions for the disciple-maker whose person has stalled, sinned, doubted, or walked away
summary: Most people quit discipling in the middle. Not at the start, when it is new and the person is eager, and not at the finish, because they never reach one. They quit in the sagging middle, when the fruit is slow and the person disappoints them and every week feels like proof that they are doing it wrong. This study is for that middle. Five sessions for the person who took someone on and now wants to give up or blame themselves. It covers the slow seed that grows while the sower sleeps, the restoring of a person who has fallen, the doubt that is not the enemy of faith, the one who walks away and the porch light you keep on, and the truth underneath all of it, that you are a sower and a servant and not the Savior. Faithfulness, not results, is the assignment.
setting: A table for the weary. Bring the real discouragement, not the tidy version you would give at church.
forWho: Anyone in the discouraging middle of discipling someone, ready to quit or blaming themselves for how slow it is going.
rhythm: Five sessions, honest and unhurried, best walked with another disciple-maker who is also in the hard middle and will tell you the truth.
leaderNote: This study exists because most people quit discipling in the middle, when the fruit is slow and the person disappoints them. If that is you, you are not failing. You are in the part nobody warned you about. Keep returning to one truth across all five sessions, and say it out loud until you believe it: you are a sower and a servant, not the Savior. You cannot make a seed grow. You cannot repent for another person. You cannot manufacture faith in someone or drag them back who has decided to leave. What you can do is stay faithful, and faithfulness, not results, is the assignment God actually gave you. Let people say the discouraging thing without rushing to fix it. The middle is a real place, and pretending it is not is why so many people quit it alone.

sessions.title: The Middle Is Always Slow
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus said the kingdom is a man who scatters seed and then sleeps and rises while the seed grows in ways he does not know and cannot hurry. The growth is real and it is hidden, which is exactly why the middle feels like nothing is happening.
sessions.open: Be honest to start: what did you expect this person to be by now, and how far is that from where they actually are?
sessions.read: Read Mark 4:26-29 out loud. And he said, The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.
observe: What does the man in the parable actually do, and just as important, what does he not do? Find every verb that belongs to him.
How does the seed grow, according to the passage? Who is making it happen while the man sleeps?
talk: The man knows not how the seed grows. He is not in charge of the growth and he cannot see it while it happens underground. How much of your discouragement comes from expecting to see growth you were never meant to see yet?
Blade, then ear, then full grain. The parable insists on stages, and none of them is skippable. Where have you been asking your person to be at full grain when they are honestly still at blade?
The man sleeps and rises night and day. He rests. What would change this week if you believed the growth did not depend on you staying anxious about it?
sessions.practice: This week, name one small blade of growth you can actually see in your person, something true even if it is nothing like the harvest you pictured. Write it down. Thank God for it out loud before you ask him for anything more.
sessions.send: The seed is growing in the dark while you sleep. Slow is not the same as dead.
sessions.passItOn: Find one other person who is discipling someone and ask them the honest question, how is the middle going. Then tell them the one blade of growth you saw this week, so they go looking for one in their own person.

sessions.title: When They Fall
sessions.bigIdea: When a person you are discipling sins, the assignment is not to drop them and it is not to pretend it did not happen. It is to restore them gently, the way Jesus restored Peter after the denial, not with a lecture but with a meal and a question and a job to do.
sessions.open: When someone you were counting on let you down, what did you want to do first, walk away or come down hard? Be honest about your gut.
sessions.read: Read Galatians 6:1. Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Then read John 21:15-17, after Peter had denied Jesus three times. Jesus said to him, Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these. He said to him, Yes, Lord, you know that I love you. He said to him, Feed my lambs. He asked him a second time, and a third, and each time gave him back the work. Tend my sheep.
observe: Paul says restore, not remove, and not excuse. What is the goal of the correction, and what is the tone he commands for it?
Jesus asks Peter three times, once for each denial, and each time hands him work to do. What does Jesus do with Peter's failure instead of rubbing his face in it?
talk: Restore is a word for setting a broken bone. It is not soft and it is not harsh, it is aimed at healing. When your person fell, did you aim at healing them or at being proven right?
Paul adds, keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Where does correcting someone tempt you toward pride, toward the quiet thought that you would never do what they did?

Jesus did not restore Peter with a speech. He fed him breakfast and gave him a job. What would it look like to restore your person with something ordinary and kind this week instead of a hard conversation about their failure?
sessions.practice: If your person has fallen, go to them this week in a spirit of gentleness, not to relitigate the sin but to hand them back a place at the table. Feed them, ask them one real question, remind them there is still work for them to do.
sessions.send: Jesus rebuilt a man who denied him with a fire and a breakfast. Restore, do not remove.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other disciple-maker about a time someone restored you gently when you had failed. Naming the person who did it for you makes you far more likely to do it for someone else.

sessions.title: When They Doubt
sessions.bigIdea: Doubt is not the enemy of faith. The man who came to Jesus said I believe, help my unbelief, in the same breath, and Jesus healed his son anyway. The table is the safest place a hard question can live, and a person who can doubt out loud with you is far less likely to doubt their way out alone.
sessions.open: What is a question about God you were once afraid to say out loud, and what happened the day you finally said it to someone?
sessions.read: Read Mark 9:23-24, where a father brings his sick son to Jesus. And Jesus said to him, If you can. All things are possible for one who believes. Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, I believe, help my unbelief. Then read Jude 22, a single short instruction for how to treat the doubting. And have mercy on those who doubt.
observe: The father says two things at once, I believe and help my unbelief. Does Jesus wait for the man to sort out his doubt before he acts, or not?
Jude gives one word for how to treat those who doubt. What is it, and what does it not say to do to them?
talk: I believe, help my unbelief, is the most honest sentence in the Gospels, and Jesus answers the prayer of a man who is only half sure. Where have you been treating your person's doubt as a failure to fix instead of a prayer to honor?
Jude says have mercy on those who doubt. Mercy, not argument, not alarm, not a stack of answers. When your person brings you a hard question, what does your face do, and is it mercy they see?

A doubt said out loud at a safe table stays inside the faith. A doubt kept silent tends to walk a person out the door quietly. How do you make your table safe enough that your person brings you the question instead of taking it somewhere else?
sessions.practice: This week, invite your person to say their hardest doubt out loud, and promise ahead of time you will not panic, argue, or fix it in one sitting. Just listen, have mercy, and say we can sit in this together. If you do not know the answer, say so, and go looking with them.
sessions.send: A doubt spoken at a safe table is not faith leaving. It is faith trying to stay.
sessions.passItOn: Tell another disciple-maker the truth, that their person's doubts are not an emergency. Pass on the one instruction from Jude, have mercy on those who doubt, and watch how it changes the way they listen.

sessions.title: When They Walk Away
sessions.bigIdea: The father in the parable let the son go. He did not chase him, guilt him, or lock the door behind him, and yet when the son came home, the father saw him a long way off, which means the father had been watching that road the whole time. You cannot force a person back. You can keep the porch light on.
sessions.open: Is there someone you poured into who walked away from the faith or from you? You do not have to name them. Just name what it did to your heart.
sessions.read: Read Luke 15:20, the turn in the story of the son who left. And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. Remember what came before this verse. The father had already let the son take his share and go. He did not stop him at the door.
observe: The father saw the son while he was still a long way off. What does that tell you about where the father had been looking during all the time the son was gone?
Notice what the father did not do when the son first demanded his share and left. What is missing, and what does its absence say about how the father held the son?
talk: The father let him go. He did not lock the door or drag him back, because love that has to be forced is not love and faith that is coerced is not faith. Where are you still trying to control an outcome that was never yours to control?
And yet the father watched the road. Letting go is not the same as giving up. What is the difference, in practice, between releasing your person and abandoning them?

The father ran. He had rehearsed that welcome a thousand times in his head while he watched the horizon. If your person came home tomorrow, would they meet a lecture about where they had been, or a father who ran?
sessions.practice: For the one who walked away, do two things this week. Release them honestly to God, out loud, admitting you cannot make them come back. Then keep the porch light on, send one word with no strings and no sermon, something as small as I am glad you exist and the door here is open.
sessions.send: You cannot drag a person home. You can be the one still watching the road when they turn onto it.
sessions.passItOn: If you know someone gutted by a person who walked away, sit with them. Do not fix it. Just remind them that the father in the story kept watching the road, and so can they, and that keeping the light on is its own kind of faithfulness.

sessions.title: You Are Not the Savior
sessions.bigIdea: Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth, so neither the planter nor the waterer is anything. The whole weight you have been carrying, the outcome, the fruit, whether the person makes it, was never yours to carry. Your assignment is the long obedience of staying faithful. God will handle what only God can do.
sessions.open: Whose faith have you secretly been holding yourself responsible for? Say the name to yourself, and then say the hard sentence, I am not their Savior.
sessions.read: Read 1 Corinthians 3:6-7. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. Then read 2 Timothy 4:7, Paul near the end of his life, measuring it. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
observe: Paul names three actors, the planter, the waterer, and God. Which jobs belong to the people, and which one belongs to God alone?
When Paul looks back over his whole life in 2 Timothy, what does he measure it by? Notice what is on the list, and what convert count or success metric is not.
talk: Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, only God who gives the growth. That is either crushing or freeing depending on the day. Which is it for you right now, and why?

Paul measured his life by fought, finished, and kept, not by how many people turned out the way he hoped. If you measured your discipling by faithfulness instead of results, would you feel like a failure or a servant who stayed?

Taking on the outcome is not humility, it is a quiet kind of pride, the belief that a person's soul rises or falls on your performance. What would you have to hand back to God this week to admit you are the servant and not the Savior?
sessions.practice: Write two lists this week. On one, everything about your person that is genuinely your job, showing up, praying, telling the truth, loving them. On the other, everything that is God's alone, the growth, the timing, the outcome, their heart. Then pray the second list back to God and stop trying to hold it.
sessions.send: You were never the Savior. That job is filled. Yours is to stay faithful and let God give the growth.
sessions.passItOn: This is the truth every disciple-maker in the hard middle needs and almost nobody says. Find one of them this week, look them in the eye, and tell them plainly, you are a sower and a servant, not the Savior, and faithfulness is the whole assignment. Then keep going, and take someone with you.
